# Physics — Class 9 (Punjab Textbook Board)

Chapter 1: Physical Quantities and Measurement

## Study notes with tables, diagrams and worked examples

## 1.1 Physics and Physical Quantities

Physics is the branch of science that deals with matter, energy and their interactions. Anything that can be measured is called a **physical quantity**. A complete measurement has two parts: a **numerical magnitude** and a **unit**. For example, in the statement “length of the table is 2 m”, 2 is the magnitude and metre (m) is the unit.

Physical quantities are divided into two groups:

• **Base quantities** — quantities that are independent of all other quantities (e.g. length, mass, time).

• **Derived quantities** — quantities obtained by combining base quantities (e.g. area, volume, speed, force).

Table 1.1: The seven SI base quantities and their units

| S. No. | Base quantity | SI unit | Symbol of unit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Length | metre | m |
| 2 | Mass | kilogram | kg |
| 3 | Time | second | s |
| 4 | Electric current | ampere | A |
| 5 | Temperature | kelvin | K |
| 6 | Amount of substance | mole | mol |
| 7 | Luminous intensity | candela | cd |

Table 1.2: Some derived quantities and their SI units

| Derived quantity | Formula | SI unit | Symbol / in base units |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Area | length × width | square metre | m<sup>2</sup> |
| Volume | length × width × height | cubic metre | m<sup>3</sup> |
| Speed | distance / time | metre per second | m s<sup>-1</sup> |
| Acceleration | change in velocity / time | metre per second squared | m s<sup>-2</sup> |
| Density | mass / volume | kilogram per cubic metre | kg m<sup>-3</sup> |
| Force | mass × acceleration | newton | N = kg m s<sup>-2</sup> |
| Pressure | force / area | pascal | Pa = N m<sup>-2</sup> |
| Work / Energy | force × distance | joule | J = N m |
| Power | work / time | watt | W = J s<sup>-1</sup> |

## 1.2 Scientific Notation (Standard Form)

Very large or very small numbers are written in the form **a × 10**<strong><sup>n</sup></strong>, where 1 ≤ a < 10 and n is an integer.

Table 1.3: Examples of scientific notation

| Quantity | Ordinary form | Scientific notation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Distance from Earth to Sun | 150 000 000 000 m | 1.5 × 1011 m |
| Mass of Earth | 5 980 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 kg | 5.98 × 1024 kg |
| Speed of light | 300 000 000 m s<sup>-1</sup> | 3 × 108 m s-1 |
| Diameter of a hydrogen atom | 0.000 000 000 1 m | 1 × 10-10 <sub>m</sub> |
| Mass of an electron | 0.000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000000 911 kg | 9.11 × 10-31 kg |

## 1.3 Prefixes

Prefixes are added before a unit to express multiples or sub-multiples of it in powers of ten.

Table 1.4: SI prefixes

| Prefix | Symbol | Power of ten | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| tera | T | 10<sup>12</sup> | 1 Tm = 10<sup>12</sup> m |
| giga | G | 10<sup>9</sup> | 1 GHz = 10<sup>9</sup> Hz |
| mega | M | 10<sup>6</sup> | 1 MW = 10<sup>6</sup> W |
| kilo | k | 10<sup>3</sup> | 1 km = 1000 m |
| deci | d | 10<sup>-1</sup> | 1 dm = 0.1 m |
| centi | c | 10<sup>-2</sup> | 1 cm = 0.01 m |
| milli | m | 10<sup>-3</sup> | 1 mm = 0.001 m |
| micro | µ | 10<sup>-6</sup> | 1 µm = 10-6 <sub>m</sub> |
| nano | n | 10<sup>-9</sup> | 1 nm = 10-9 <sub>m</sub> |
| pico | p | 10-12 | 1 pF = 10-12 <sub>F</sub> |

## 1.4 Measuring Instruments

Choosing the right instrument depends on the size of the object and the accuracy needed.

Table 1.5: Common measuring instruments

| Instrument | Measures | Least count | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Metre rule | Length | 1 mm = 0.1 cm | Length of a book, table |
| Vernier callipers | Length, inner/outer diameter, depth | 0.1 mm = 0.01 cm | Diameter of a test tube |
| Screw gauge | Very small lengths, thickness | 0.01 mm = 0.001 cm | Thickness of wire, thin sheet |
| Physical balance | Mass | 1 mg (0.001 g) | Mass of small objects |
| Measuring cylinder | Volume of liquid | 1 mL (typical) | Volume of a liquid or irregular solid |
| Stop watch | Time interval | 0.1 s or 0.01 s | Time period of a pendulum |

## 1.4.1 Vernier Callipers

A vernier callipers has a main scale (M.S.) and a sliding vernier scale (V.S.). Ten divisions of the vernier scale are equal to nine divisions of the main scale.

## Least count (L.C.) = 1 M.S.D − 1 V.S.D = 1 mm − 0.9 mm = 0.1 mm = 0.01 cm

**Total reading = M.S. reading + (V.S. coincidence number × L.C.)**

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 1.1: Vernier scale reading. Example: M.S. reading = 2.3 cm, coinciding division = 6, so reading = 2.3 + 6 × 0.01 = 2.36 cm.

## Zero error and zero correction

If the zero of the vernier scale does not coincide with the zero of the main scale when the jaws are closed, the instrument has a **zero error**.

Table 1.6: Zero error rules

| Case | Zero error | Zero correction | Corrected reading |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Zero of V.S. is ahead of zero of M.S. (positive error) | + e | - e | Observed reading - e |
| Zero of V.S. is behind zero of M.S. (negative error) | - e | + e | Observed reading + e |
| Both zeros coincide | 0 | 0 | Observed reading |

## 1.4.2 Screw Gauge

A screw gauge works on the principle of a screw. The **pitch** is the distance moved by the screw in one complete rotation.

## Least count = pitch / number of divisions on circular scale = 1 mm / 100 = 0.01 mm

## Total reading = linear scale reading + (circular scale reading × L.C.)

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 1.2: Parts of a screw gauge (schematic).

## 1.4.3 Measuring Cylinder

A measuring cylinder is used to find the volume of a liquid. The eye must be kept at the level of the lower meniscus to avoid parallax error. The volume of an irregular solid is found by the change in liquid level when it is fully immersed.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 1.3: Reading the volume with a measuring cylinder.

## 1.5 Significant Figures

Significant figures are the reliably known digits in a measurement plus one estimated digit. They show the precision of a measurement.

Table 1.7: Rules for counting significant figures

| Rule | Example | No. of sig. figs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| All non-zero digits are significant | 432.5 m | 4 |
| Zeros between non-zero digits are significant | 2005 kg | 4 |
| Leading zeros are not significant | 0.0045 m | 2 |
| Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant | 3.200 s | 4 |
| Trailing zeros without a decimal point are not always significant | 4500 m | 2 (or more, if specified) |
| Scientific notation shows sig. figs clearly | 6.30 × 10<sup>3</sup> m | 3 |

## 1.6 Precision and Accuracy

• **Precision** — how close repeated measurements are to each other. It depends on the least count of the instrument.

• **Accuracy** — how close a measurement is to the true (accepted) value.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 1.4: Accuracy versus precision, shown as shots on a target.

Table 1.8: Example — five measurements of a rod whose true length is 10.00 cm

| Trial | Student A (cm) | Student B (cm) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 10.01 | 9.60 |
| 2 | 9.99 | 9.61 |
| 3 | 10.00 | 9.59 |
| 4 | 10.02 | 9.60 |
| 5 | 9.98 | 9.60 |
| Mean | 10.00 | 9.60 |
| Conclusion | Accurate and precise | Precise but not accurate |

## 1.7 Worked Examples

**Example 1.** Convert 72 km h<sup>-1</sup> into m s-1.

72 km h<sup>-1</sup> = 72 × 1000 m / 3600 s = 20 m s-1

**Example 2.** A wire has diameter 0.52 mm. Write it in metres using scientific notation. 0.52 mm = 0.52 × 10<sup>-3</sup> m = 5.2 × 10<sup>-4</sup> m

**Example 3.** A screw gauge has zero error +0.03 mm. Its observed reading for a wire is 1.78 mm. Find the corrected reading.

Corrected reading = 1.78 − 0.03 = 1.75 mm
